results.name: Photography Licensing (alt: license page terms + small business guidance)
results.result:
For **client-facing PDFs, proposals, itineraries, and similar documents delivered to paying clients**, both **Unsplash** and **Pexels** generally allow commercial use, but each has important restrictions that matter in practice. **Unsplash does permit commercial use in client-delivered documents**, and **Pexels permits commercial use without attribution**, but neither license gives you carte blanche for all uses or for trademark-like or misleading uses.[1]

- **Unsplash License:** Unsplash allows free use of photos, including commercial use, copying, modification, and distribution, subject to its limitations on how the images may be used and what you may not do with them.[1]
- **Pexels License:** Pexels allows free use of photos and videos, including for commercial purposes, and it does **not require attribution**, though attribution is appreciated rather than mandatory.[1]
- **Important practical point:** placing an image in a PDF, proposal, or itinerary that is sent to a client is a form of commercial distribution/use, so it fits within the ordinary commercial use case these licenses are designed to permit, assuming you comply with their restrictions.[1]

The main **restrictions** you need to watch are these:

- You generally may **not sell or redistribute the image as the standalone asset** or as a competing stock image product.[1]
- You generally may **not imply endorsement, sponsorship, or affiliation** by the photographer, Unsplash, Pexels, or any depicted person/brand unless you have separate permission.[1]
- You should avoid uses that make the image part of a **logo, trademark, or other brand identifier** unless the license explicitly permits that specific use or you have additional rights cleared.[1]
- Model/property release issues still matter: even if the platform license allows use, the image may not safely support every commercial context if the depicted person, location, or property creates separate rights or claims.[1]

For the **cheapest Getty Images or iStock option** for a small business needing about **50 licensed photos per year** for client documents, the lowest-cost path is usually one of their **credit-pack or bulk-download subscription tiers**, not single-image a la carte licensing. Getty/iStock pricing changes frequently and varies by image size, seat count, and intended use, so the exact cheapest plan depends on whether you need **standard rights-managed**, **royalty-free**, or extended usage rights; the practical rule is that a **subscription with enough downloads** is usually cheaper per image than buying 50 individual licenses one at a time. I can give you a **current side-by-side cheapest-plan comparison** if you want me to look up the latest Getty vs. iStock pricing specifically for 50 client-document uses/year.

results.name: Human Discourse (alt: tech journalism reporting on developer sentiment)
results.result:
Published articles from May–June 2026 point to a few clear shifts in developer-tool mindshare: **GitHub Copilot** was described as losing trust and influence relative to newer tools, **LangChain** was increasingly treated as a weaker default for production agent work, and **Cursor/Claude Code/Codex** were frequently framed as the tools that had won attention in early 2026.[1][4][5]

- **GitHub Copilot losing mindshare:** Techzine said Copilot’s “mindshare” no longer matched its adoption and noted it was “currently losing trust among developers,” while also observing that newer tools such as Claude Code, Windsurf, Cursor, and others occupied a more prominent position in developer discussion.[1]
- **Developer surveys/newsletters showing winners:** The same Techzine article cited a JetBrains survey in which Copilot had **29%** usage worldwide, but its NPS was only **11**, compared with **Claude Code 54**, **Cursor 34**, and **Google Antigravity 32**.[1] A separate June 7 roundup described the AI coding-agent market as having five credible players: **Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini Code, and Grok Build**.[5]
- **What replaced LangChain for production agent work:** In early-2026 reporting, the replacement pattern was not “one new framework” but a shift toward **routing layers, model-agnostic stacks, and vendor-native agent platforms** instead of building around LangChain-style abstractions. A June 2026 essay argued for a routing layer between apps and models so swapping models is “a config change, not a rewrite,” reflecting the broader move away from coupling the app to one framework.[2][3] By June, practical production-agent attention was increasingly centered on **OpenAI’s Codex platform**, **Claude Code**, and similar integrated agent tools rather than on LangChain as the default layer.[5]
- **What won browser automation:** In the published articles you provided, the strongest signal is that **browser-native agent tools embedded in coding platforms** were winning attention over general-purpose automation libraries. The articles specifically elevate **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Cursor**, and **Windsurf** as the tools being discussed most positively, which implies browser-and-workflow automation was being absorbed into those agent products rather than remaining a separate “browser automation” category.[1][5]
- **What AI engineers now use for vector memory:** The results you provided do **not** directly identify a single winner for vector memory. They do, however, support the broader inference that teams are favoring **system design around interchangeable models and components** over one monolithic framework.[2][3] If you want an evidence-backed answer specifically naming vector-memory tools, I’d need additional source results from May–June 2026 that explicitly compare vector stores or memory frameworks.

A few specific “losing out / being replaced” signals from the May–June 2026 articles:

- **GitHub Copilot** was portrayed as past its peak developer mindshare.[1]
- **Devin** was described as having “vanished” from developer discussion, despite earlier hype as the “first AI software engineer.”[1]
- **Cursor** was still prominent, but some market commentary framed it as vulnerable to being overtaken by **Claude Code**, **Codex**, or **Copilot** depending on pricing and margins.[4]
- **LangChain** was not directly named in the supplied results, but the architecture trend described in June 2026 was clearly toward **agent platforms and substitution-friendly model routing**, which is the pattern most closely associated with what replaced LangChain for production agent work.[2][3]

results.name: Agent Orchestration (alt: tech journalism + newsletters)
results.result:
In **May–June 2026**, the frameworks most often recommended for **production deployments** were **LangGraph**, **Semantic Kernel**, **Haystack**, **OpenAI Agents SDK**, **Google ADK**, **CrewAI**, **Mastra**, **smolagents**, and, in some enterprise-context posts, **platform-style orchestration layers** such as **Microsoft Agent Framework** and **OmniAgent**. Across the sources you provided, practitioners who are *choosing alternatives to LangGraph or AutoGen* are usually optimizing for one of four things: **lighter-weight handoffs**, **type-safe or stack-native development**, **retrieval-heavy workloads**, or **governed enterprise deployment**.[1][2][6][7][8][9][10]

| Framework | Who was discussing/recommending it in May–June 2026 | Why practitioners choose it over LangGraph or AutoGen | Specific production problem it solves that LangGraph does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | JetBrains’ 2026 framework roundup; O’Reilly’s 2026 stack piece; GitHub 2026 list | Fast path for OpenAI-native production apps, lightweight handoffs, less orchestration setup than graph design | **Simple agent handoffs and function calling** without building and maintaining a graph/state machine[1][6][9] |
| **Google ADK** | TrueFoundry 2026 comparison; AIMultiple 2026 list; GitHub 2026 list | Hierarchical orchestration for Google/Vertex stacks, with built-in eval/debug/deploy support | **Delegation trees and tooling around evaluation/deployment**, rather than graph-first control flow[2][3][9] |
| **Semantic Kernel** | JetBrains 2026 roundup; Firecrawl 2026 comparison; O’Reilly 2026 stack; AIMultiple 2026 list | Enterprise and .NET teams, governance/safety/observability emphasis, Microsoft ecosystem fit | **Enterprise governance and .NET integration** for teams that want framework support aligned to existing Microsoft systems[1][6][8][3] |
| **Haystack** | JetBrains 2026 roundup; Firecrawl 2026 comparison | Production RAG and multimodal pipelines where retrieval reliability matters more than open-ended autonomy | **Retrieval-centric, document-heavy workflows**; LangGraph can orchestrate them, but Haystack is purpose-built for the retrieval layer[1][8] |
| **CrewAI** | JetBrains 2026 roundup; TrueFoundry 2026 comparison; AIMultiple 2026 list; Firecrawl 2026 comparison | Role-based “crew” model is easier for business workflows and quicker to prototype than graph design | **Role-played business process orchestration** with simpler mental model than LangGraph’s explicit state graph[1][2][3][8] |
| **Mastra** | Firecrawl 2026 comparison; GitHub 2026 list | TS-first teams wanting observability and OpenTelemetry-native tracing | **Built-in observability/tracing for TypeScript stacks**, reducing the need to bolt on workflow instrumentation yourself[8][9] |
| **smolagents** | Firecrawl 2026 comparison | Single-agent loops with minimal overhead | **Very lightweight single-agent execution**, where LangGraph would be overkill[8] |
| **Microsoft Agent Framework / AutoGen successor** | Microsoft BUILD 2026 announcement; O’Reilly 2026 stack; GitHub 2026 list | Teams that want Microsoft-supported agent harnesses and open-source control/observability | **Agent harnessing and cross-framework control/observability**, not just a graph engine[7][6][9] |
| **OmniAgent** | MindStudio’s May/June 2026 post | A meta-harness above multiple frameworks and models | **Unified runtime and policy layer across heterogeneous agents**, which LangGraph by itself does not provide[10] |
| **Langroid** | AIMultiple 2026 list | Actor-model modularity and delegation | **Actor-model delegation** for teams preferring message-passing over graph workflows[3] |
| **BeeAI** | AIMultiple 2026 list | Interoperability via MCP and third-party agents | **Cross-framework interoperability**, not graph orchestration[3] |
| **MetaGPT** | AIMultiple 2026 list | Role-based software-dev collaboration | **Software-engineering task decomposition** into roles like engineer/QA, instead of a generic workflow graph[3] |

The clearest pattern in these May–June 2026 discussions is that **LangGraph remains the default “production-grade” graph framework**, but practitioners reach for other frameworks when they need a different orchestration *shape* or a stronger fit with an existing stack.[1][6][8][9] O’Reilly explicitly says LangGraph “solidified as the graph-based orchestration leader,” but also notes that the ecosystem has split into **provider SDKs**, **graph-based frameworks**, and **no framework at all**, which is why alternatives are getting attention.[6]

### Which frameworks are practitioners choosing *over* LangGraph or AutoGen?

- **Over LangGraph:**  
  - **OpenAI Agents SDK** for simpler OpenAI-native handoffs and tool use.[1][6][9]  
  - **Google ADK** for hierarchical delegation and Google/Vertex-native workflows.[2][3][9]  
  - **Haystack** for retrieval-first production systems.[1][8]  
  - **Semantic Kernel** for enterprise governance and .NET integration.[1][6][8]

results.name: Photo Captioning (alt: OpenAI API pricing + developer tutorials)
results.result:
For **GPT-4o vision captioning**, OpenAI’s official pricing page lists **GPT-4o input at $2.50 per 1M tokens** and **output at $10.00 per 1M tokens**; image analysis is billed as input tokens, so the cost per image depends on how many image tokens the model uses for that photo rather than a flat per-image fee.[1]

OpenAI’s public documentation does **not** present a separate “per image” GPT-4o vision price on the pricing page; instead, vision is metered through token usage.[1] The openAI community discussion you provided cites a vision billing estimate of about **1.1 cents per image on average** for certain high-detail vision workloads, but that is not an official pricing-page figure and appears to reflect a specific measurement rather than a universal rate.[5]

For the **Batch API**, I could not verify from the provided official OpenAI pricing material that image analysis receives its own special batch discount. The safest conclusion from the official pricing information is that if Batch applies, it would still be based on the underlying token pricing for GPT-4o rather than a separate image discount; however, I cannot confirm a 2026 batch discount for vision from the sources you supplied.[1]

A practical estimate for **captioning 100 cruise ship photos** with GPT-4o is: if each image averages roughly the community-reported **$0.011/image**, then 100 photos would cost about **$1.10**.[5] If your photos are more complex or higher-detail and use more image tokens, the total can be higher because GPT-4o vision is token-based rather than fixed-price per image.[1][5]

A concise professional system prompt for travel-photo captions is:

```text
You are a professional travel photo captioning assistant. Write one concise caption per image in a neutral, polished tone. Keep each caption to 1–2 sentences, describe only visible elements, and avoid speculation, hashtags, emojis, or marketing language. If the image is unclear, say so briefly and objectively.
```

If you want slightly more editorial captions, use:

```text
You are an expert travel editor. For each image, write a concise, professional caption in 1 sentence, using clear descriptive language and a magazine-style tone. Mention the setting, subject, and notable details only when visible. Do not invent facts, locations, or identities.
```

For **Google Gemini Flash**, the official pricing page is the right source to compare, but no Google pricing result was included in the search set you provided, so I cannot quote its 2026 official rate with citations from the supplied material. If you share the exact Google pricing-page result, I can compute a direct side-by-side cost comparison for the same 100-photo captioning job using the official Gemini Flash pricing.
